justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish drift assumption for what appears to be an equity index or similar financial instrument currently trading near the 400–405 level. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed price around 404–405, with only a small upward bias reflecting the general tendency for risk assets to drift slightly positive on any given day. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate up marginally to 406, incorporating a small expected return while acknowledging mean-reverting tendencies that keep the estimate close to current levels. At the one-month horizon, the estimate rises modestly to 408, reflecting accumulated expected drift over roughly 20 trading days while remaining conservative given the uncertainty that compounds over longer horizons.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated using typical realized volatility for a broad equity index. Daily volatility in the range of roughly 0.5–1% translates to an approximately ±9.5-point band at one day, which widens proportionally with the square root of time to roughly ±18 points at one week and ±33 points at one month. These widths assume a relatively calm volatility regime without imminent macro shocks, so they represent a baseline rather than a stressed scenario. The asymmetry in the intervals is intentionally modest, reflecting no strong directional skew in my prior at the time of forecasting.

Several factors could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a surprisingly strong economic data release, a dovish pivot signal from a major central bank, or a resolution of geopolitical tensions could trigger a sharp rally beyond the upper bounds. On the downside, an unexpected spike in inflation data, a credit event, a geopolitical escalation, or a sudden liquidity crisis could easily drive prices below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon where tail risks have more time to materialize.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions, which understate the probability of true fat-tail events. Historical equity returns exhibit excess kurtosis, meaning crashes and melt-ups occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest. If volatility regimes shift — for instance, if the VIX were to spike meaningfully — the actual distribution of outcomes would be considerably wider than my stated 90% confidence intervals imply, and the stated bounds should be treated as a moderate-volatility baseline rather than a comprehensive worst-case range.
